what_it_does: Modern computers sometimes expand their working memory by connecting solid-state drives (SSDs — the flash storage chips common in laptops) over a high-speed link called CXL (think of CXL as a very fast cable that lets the processor treat remote storage almost like local memory). The problem is that flash storage is much slower than regular memory chips, and it also has unpredictable 'garbage collection' pauses — moments when the drive reorganizes its internal data, freezing normal access. This paper redesigns how the operating system and the SSD work together to hide those delays: when the processor is stuck waiting on a slow SSD access, the operating system immediately switches to running a different program thread instead of sitting idle; a small buffer inside the SSD quietly collects many tiny writes and batches them into larger ones to reduce wasteful back-and-forth; and frequently-touched data gets automatically promoted to fast local memory chips (DRAM — the standard high-speed volatile memory in a PC). The combined result is that programs see dramatically fewer stall cycles and the SSD performs far less redundant work.
